In [[mathematics|mathematical]] [[set theory]], '''Baumgartner's axiom (BA)''' can be one of three different [[axiom]]s introduced by [[James Earl Baumgartner]].

A subset of the [[real line]] is said to be <math>\aleph_1</math>-[[dense set|dense]] if every two points are separated by exactly <math>\aleph_1</math> other points, where <math>\aleph_1</math> is the [[Aleph number|smallest uncountable cardinality]]. This would be true for the real line itself under the [[continuum hypothesis]]. An axiom introduced by {{harvtxt|Baumgartner|1973}} states that all <math>\aleph_1</math>-[[dense set|dense]] subsets of the [[real line]] are [[order-isomorphic]], providing a higher-cardinality analogue of [[Cantor's isomorphism theorem]] that countable dense subsets are isomorphic. Baumgartner's axiom is a consequence of the [[proper forcing axiom]]. It is consistent with a combination of [[ZFC]], [[Martin's axiom]], and the negation of the [[continuum hypothesis]],<ref>{{citation|last=Baumgartner|first=James E.|doi=10.4064/fm-79-2-101-106|issue=2|journal=Fundamenta Mathematicae|mr=317934|pages=101–106|title=All <math>\aleph_{1}</math>-dense sets of reals can be isomorphic|volume=79|year=1973|doi-access=free}}</ref> but not implied by those hypotheses.<ref>{{citation|last1=Avraham|first1=Uri|last2=Shelah|first2=Saharon|author2-link=Saharon Shelah|doi=10.1007/BF02761858|issue=1–2|journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]|mr=599485|pages=161–176|title=Martin's axiom does not imply that every two <math>\aleph_{1}</math>-dense sets of reals are isomorphic|volume=38|year=1981}}</ref>

Another axiom introduced by {{harvtxt|Baumgartner|1975}} states that [[Martin's axiom]] for [[partially ordered set]]s MA<sub>''P''</sub>(''κ'') is true for all [[partially ordered set]]s ''P'' that are countable closed, well met and ℵ<sub>1</sub>-linked and all [[Cardinal number|cardinals]] κ less than 2<sup>ℵ<sub>1</sub></sup>.

Baumgartner's '''axiom A''' is an axiom for partially ordered sets introduced in {{harv|Baumgartner|1983|loc=section 7}}. A partial order (''P'',&nbsp;≤) is said to satisfy axiom A if there is a family ≤<sub>''n''</sub> of partial orderings on ''P'' for ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;2,&nbsp;... such that 
# ≤<sub>0</sub> is the same as&nbsp;≤
#If ''p''&nbsp;≤<sub>''n''+1</sub>''q'' then ''p''&nbsp;≤<sub>''n''</sub>''q''
#If there is a sequence ''p''<sub>''n''</sub> with ''p''<sub>''n''+1</sub>&nbsp;≤<sub>''n''</sub> ''p''<sub>''n''</sub> then there is a ''q'' with ''q''&nbsp;≤<sub>''n''</sub> ''p''<sub>''n''</sub> for all ''n''.
#If ''I'' is a pairwise incompatible subset of ''P'' then for all ''p'' and for all natural numbers ''n'' there is a ''q'' such that ''q''&nbsp;≤<sub>''n''</sub> ''p'' and the number of elements of ''I'' compatible with ''q'' is countable.
